IDK
EYE-dee-KAY
interjection (Millennial slang)
Initialism for I don’t know, from 1990s chat and 2000s texting, where it became the all-purpose shrug: ignorance, indecision, indifference, or a refusal to commit ("idk, whatever you want"). Related forms: idek (I don’t even know), idc (I don’t care), idrk (I don’t really know), and the typed shrug emoticon, popular from about 2011.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

IDK is the typed shrug. Sometimes it is simple honesty: I do not know the answer. Sometimes it is something else wearing honesty’s clothes: I do not want to decide, I do not want to think about it, I do not care enough to find out. The Christian observation separates the two. An honest "I don’t know" is a mark of wisdom and humility. Job, after all his speeches, confessed: "therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not" (Job 42:3). Scripture honours the man who admits the edge of his knowledge, and it insists that some things belong to God alone: "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever" (Deu 29:29). But the second half of that verse is a charge. What God has revealed, we are meant to know, and the shrug is no answer to the questions He has answered. Peter tells every believer to "be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you" (1Pe 3:15). "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God" (Jas 1:5). A father welcomes his child’s honest "I don’t know" and answers it with "let’s find out." He gently refuses the lazy "idk" on matters that need a decision, and he makes sure his children know what they believe and why.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial text initialism (1990s–2000s) for I don’t know; honest humility when it marks the edge of knowledge (Deu 29:29), sloth when it shrugs off what God has revealed and asks us to answer (1Pe 3:15).

IDK, interj. (Millennial text slang, 1990s–present; initialism of I don’t know) Ignorance, uncertainty, or reluctance to decide. Related: idek, idc, idrk, the shrug emoticon.

Webster (1828), root know: KNOW, verb transitive no. preterit tense knew; participle passive known. [Latin nosco, cognosco, Gr. although much varied in orthography. Nosco makes novi, which, with g or c prefixed, gnovi or cnovi, would coincide with know knew. So Latin cresco, crevi, coincides with grow, grew. The radical sense of knowing is generally to take, receive, or hold.] 1. To perceive with certainty; to understand clearly; to have a clear and certain perception of truth, fact, or any thing that actually exists. […]

Decode for parents: answer an honest idk with "let’s find out"; do not accept idk on what they believe.

Key Scripture

Job 42:3 — "Who is he that hideth counsel without knowledge? therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not."

Deu 29:29 — "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law."

1Pe 3:15 — "But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:"

Jas 1:5 — "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him."

Pro 2:3-5 — "Yea, if thou criest after knowledge, and liftest up thy voice for understanding; If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures; Then shalt thou understand the fear of the LORD, and find the knowledge of God."

Modern Corruption

IDK can be humble honesty or a lazy shrug; Scripture honours the first and rebukes the second, because what God has revealed belongs to us and our children.

expand to see more

The drift is from honest ignorance to cultivated indifference. A generation with every fact in its pocket answers more questions with a shrug than any before it, because the shrug is not about information; it is about will. "I don’t know" becomes "don’t make me think," and in matters of faith it becomes a permanent posture: idk what I believe, idk if it matters. That is not humility. It is the sluggard’s answer to wisdom’s invitation.

Scripture’s remedy is the search. "If thou criest after knowledge, and liftest up thy voice for understanding; If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures; Then shalt thou understand the fear of the LORD, and find the knowledge of God" (Pro 2:3-5). Teach the young that it is good to say "I don’t know," and better to follow it with prayer, study, and the courage to come to a conviction. Leave the secret things with God; take the revealed things home.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English cnawan (to know) → "I don’t know" → 1990s chat initialism idk → 2000s texting shrug (idek, idc).

Old English cnawan — to perceive, to recognize

1990s: chat initialism idk

2000s: texting; idek, idc, idrk

c. 2011: shrug emoticon as the visual idk

Biblical anchor: the secret things belong unto the LORD (Deu 29:29); be ready always to give an answer (1Pe 3:15)

Usage

""Where do you want to eat?" "idk, wherever.""

"An honest idk is humble; a permanent one about the gospel is not (1Pe 3:15)."

"If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God (Jas 1:5)."
